# Automated Detection of Pork-Rasher Packaging and Placement Defects

**MMA3001 Numerical Methods and Machine Learning — Individual Project Report**
Author: Haruku Nishikawa · Co-author: Claude (Anthropic) · Repository: `rasher-qc` · October 2026

*Every number below is generated by the code (`results/<dataset>/SUMMARY.md`, `results/<dataset>/tables/operating_points.json`); nothing was typed in by hand. Real-data models were trained on my laptop (RTX 4070 laptop GPU, 20-thread Intel CPU, Windows 11). `-block` is the leakage-aware split and `-reduced` the predefined one (Section 2.2).*

## 1. Engineering problem

**Context.** Bacon is packed by laying rashers in a plastic tray and heat-sealing a lidding film onto the tray's flange. Both steps go wrong. Rashers end up *loose* (out of place, hanging over the edge) or *twisted*; the film ends up *unsealed* along part of the flange, *wrinkled*, or damaged in some other way (*packaging-error*). An unsealed pack leaks, loses its protective atmosphere and spoils early; a messy one gets sent back by the retailer. Most lines still check this by eye, one person watching about a tray a second. That is tiring, it drifts over a shift, and it leaves no record.

**What I set out to do.** From one top-view RGB photo of a sealed tray: (1) **find and box** every defect of the five labelled types; (2) **decide** whether the tray passes, fails, or goes to a person (PASS / FAIL / REVIEW); (3) **find out** whether that is accurate and fast enough for a line, and how far the accuracy numbers can be trusted.

**Why it matters and intended use.** The two mistakes don't cost the same: letting an unsealed pack through is a food-safety and recall problem, failing a good pack costs a second look. So I judge the system mainly by how many defective trays it catches for a given rate of good trays wrongly failed. It is meant as a helper at the end of the line, not a replacement for the operator: clear passes go through, clear fails are diverted, the uncertain middle goes to a person, and every tray gets a machine-readable record (`results.json`).

**Out of scope.** Only the five labelled defects and this dataset's camera set-up (fixed overhead camera, dark textured belt, clear trays, 720 × 540 images). No leak testing (a seal can look fine and still leak), no weight or slice counts, no hardware integration, no claims about other products or lighting.

## 2. Inputs, outputs and data

### 2.1 Top-level inputs and outputs

| | Item | Format, units, domain | Meaning and use |
|---|---|---|---|
| In | Tray image | RGB, uint8 (0–255), 720 × 540 px (accepted 240–8192 px per side); one tray, top view | The only run-time input |
| In | Training data | YOLO export (class, centre x, centre y, width, height, normalised 0–1) or COCO JSON (pixels) | Training and evaluation only |
| Out | Decision | `PASS`, `REVIEW`, `FAIL`, `UNSUPPORTED_INPUT` | What the line does with the tray |
| Out | Tray score | 0–1, highest defect confidence | Ranking; setting thresholds |
| Out | Defect list | class; confidence 0–1; box x1, y1, x2, y2 in pixels; box area as fraction of image | Where to look; rough severity |
| Out | Run report | `results.json`, annotated JPEGs, `summary.html` | Traceability, supervisor overview |

**Bad or unsupported inputs** (`rasherqc.io.validate_image`). I'd rather the system admit it can't read an image than guess. Missing or undecodable files, greyscale images, RGB images with identical channels, images too small to resolve a crease (< 240 px), and badly exposed images (mean grey outside 20–235, or > 25 % of pixels clipped) come back as `UNSUPPORTED_INPUT` with the reason, and are never passed automatically. RGBA is accepted with a warning. Unknown class ids or malformed label lines raise an error. Function-level inputs and outputs are in the docstrings and the generated HTML API docs (`docs/api/`).

### 2.2 The dataset, and what the audit turned up

*Pork Rasher Error (Packaging)* (Roboflow Universe, v4, CC BY 4.0): 3,349 training images (three exposure-shifted copies of 1,085 source frames), 120 validation and 80 test images at 720 × 540, with boxes for five classes. Auditing it before training changed the project in three ways.

1. **The images are video frames, and the predefined split leaks.** The file names give it away (`frame_with_red_<n>`). The median distance from a test image to the nearest training frame is **2.5 frames** (3 for validation); 57 % of test images are within 3 frames of one, all within 30, and 5 % share the exact frame number. A "test" tray is usually the *same physical tray* a fraction of a second later. A perceptual-hash check flagged 143 validation/test images as near-duplicates of training images.
2. **The classes are badly imbalanced.** Training has 1,712 `packaging-error`, 1,055 `unsealed`, 72 `twisted-meat`, 66 `loose-meat` and 18 `wrinkle` boxes; validation and test have no `wrinkle` and 3–4 of each of the other two. I call a class *evaluable* only with at least 10 test boxes, which leaves `packaging-error` and `unsealed`.
3. **Hardly any good trays to test on.** Only 12 of the 80 test images have no defect, so a false-reject rate measured there is very uncertain.

**What I did about it.** The code builds two dataset versions. The **predefined split (`-reduced`)** keeps the given split but only one copy per training frame (the detector does its own, wider colour augmentation). The **block split (`-block`)** cuts all frames into blocks of 300 consecutive frame numbers, assigns whole blocks to test or validation, and drops training frames within 60 frames of a held-out one: 872 training, 155 validation and 173 test frames, with 98 `packaging-error` and 51 `unsealed` test boxes and 39 good test trays. Running everything on both splits measures how optimistic the predefined split is (Section 5.4).

![Examples of each class (training split)](../results/pork-rasher/figures/examples.png){width=100%}

### 2.3 Synthetic verification dataset

A generator (`rasherqc.synthetic`) draws tray images in the same format and class list with **exactly correct boxes**, the image-processing version of a manufactured solution: if the pipeline can't score perfect labels perfectly, the bug is in my code. It says nothing about real trays (which look quite different), so it is used for verification only.

## 3. Computational solution

**Pipeline:** image → input validation → YOLOv8n detector → boxes and confidences → tray score *s* = highest defect confidence → PASS / REVIEW / FAIL → report.

**How YOLOv8 works.** It is a one-stage, anchor-free convolutional detector. A CSP-Darknet backbone with C2f blocks extracts feature maps at strides 8, 16 and 32, and a path-aggregation neck mixes them so that small defects (a lifted film corner) and large ones (a loose rasher) are both represented. A decoupled head predicts, for every cell, class probabilities and the distances to the four box edges as small probability distributions. Training minimises binary cross-entropy (classes) + CIoU (box overlap) + distribution focal loss (edges), with a task-aligned assigner matching cells to ground truth, using AdamW. The weights kept are from the epoch with the best validation fitness (0.1·mAP@0.5 + 0.9·mAP@0.5:0.95); early stopping ends training after 15 epochs without improvement. Non-maximum suppression (IoU 0.6) removes duplicate boxes.

**Why this method.** It *localises*, which the brief asks for and an operator needs. One forward pass per image suits a line at about a tray a second, and the nano model (3.0 M parameters) runs on a CPU (Section 6). COCO-pretrained weights reuse generic edge and texture features, useful with only 1,085 distinct frames, a claim I test directly (Section 4). The data is already boxed, and the library is widely used and runs the same on CPU and GPU.

**Assumptions.** A defect is visible in one top-view frame; box labels are consistent enough to learn from; all splits come from the same camera, belt and trays; a tray's status is summed up by its most confident defect.

**Settings.** Input 416 px (long side); 60 epochs on the GPU; batch 16; AdamW, learning rate ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻³ (auto); patience 15; seed 42, `deterministic=True`. Augmentation: mosaic (off for the last 5 epochs), horizontal and vertical flips (a camera looking straight down has no "up"), HSV jitter; no rotation, since trays always run along the belt. One implementation trap: Ultralytics expects BGR images and my code is RGB. Get it wrong and nothing crashes, red meat just quietly turns blue, so a unit test checks that an array and a file give identical detections.

**Tray decision.** FAIL if *s* ≥ *t*<sub>fail</sub>, REVIEW if *t*<sub>low</sub> ≤ *s* < *t*<sub>fail</sub>, otherwise PASS. Both thresholds are set on the **validation** split: *t*<sub>fail</sub> is the highest threshold that still catches 95 % of defective validation trays, *t*<sub>low</sub> the highest that catches 99 %. These targets encode the lopsided costs; a plant would set its own.

**Known limitations.** Boxes are axis-aligned, so box area overstates defect area (fine for ranking, not measuring). The model can't find what it has barely seen (6 `wrinkle` training boxes after de-duplication). Confidences aren't calibrated probabilities, so a new camera or product needs new thresholds. Ultralytics is AGPL-3.0, so a closed commercial version would need a licence or another detector.

## 4. Alternative solutions

I compared three methods, all producing a 0–1 tray score and passing through the same threshold procedure, so their tray decisions compare like for like. **A** is the main method. **B** is the same YOLOv8n trained from scratch (same data, settings and seed), which tests whether pretraining pays off. **C** is a classical baseline: 80 hand-crafted colour, texture, morphological and orientation features feeding a 500-tree random forest tuned by 5-fold cross-validation. Its features follow the physics of each defect: parallel rashers give coherent edge orientations and a loose one adds a second direction; wrinkles and lifted film edges are thin bright lines (white top-hat); an unsealed flange shows a dark gap (black top-hat); a 3 × 3 spatial pyramid stops small defects being averaged away.

**Table 1. Test-split comparison.** Leakage-aware block split (173 trays: 134 defective, 39 good), predefined split in brackets (80 trays: 68 / 12). Thresholds chosen on validation; 95 % bootstrap CIs.

| | A: YOLOv8n pretrained | B: YOLOv8n scratch | C: features + RF |
|---|---|---|---|
| mAP@0.5 / mAP@0.5:0.95, evaluable classes | **0.783 / 0.387** (0.589 / 0.317) | 0.654 / 0.314 (0.482 / 0.294) | — |
| AP@0.5 `unsealed` / `packaging-error` | 0.871 / **0.696** (0.851 / 0.328) | 0.827 / 0.481 (0.840 / 0.125) | — |
| Tray ROC AUC | **0.862** [0.78, 0.92] (0.924) | 0.855 [0.79, 0.91] (0.908) | 0.673 [0.57, 0.76] (0.763) |
| False-reject rate at FAIL recall ≈ 0.90 † | **0.41** [0.26, 0.56] (0.08) | 0.44 [0.28, 0.59] (0.08) | 0.74 [0.61, 0.87] (0.50) |
| False-reject rate at FAIL recall ≈ 0.80 † | **0.18** [0.06, 0.31] (0.08) | 0.23 [0.10, 0.37] (0.08) | 0.54 [0.39, 0.69] (0.33) |
| Validation thresholds: escape / review / false-reject | 1.5 % / 2.9 % / 56 % | 0.7 % / 3.5 % / 80 % | 0.7 % / 2.9 % / 92 % |
| CPU latency per tray, mean (p95) | 63 ms (80) | same model size | 385 ms |
| Training cost; labels needed | 30 min GPU; boxes | 14–35 min GPU; boxes | 3 min CPU; image labels |

† Read off the test ROC to show the trade-off; decision thresholds are only ever chosen on validation.

![Tray ROC, block split](../results/pork-rasher-block/figures/tray_roc.png){width=48%} ![Operating points, block split](../results/pork-rasher-block/figures/operating_points.png){width=48%}

**Which one, and why.** I picked the pretrained detector (A): it is best or tied-best on every accuracy measure on both splits. Pretraining matters most on the hard class, `packaging-error` (AP 0.70 vs 0.48 on the block split, 0.33 vs 0.13 on the predefined one); `unsealed`, big and high-contrast, is learned almost as well from scratch. To be fair to B, its validation curve was still rising at epoch 60 (best epoch 54) while A had levelled off (best epoch 49), so part of the gap is training budget; at equal budget, pretraining wins. The baseline (C) isn't good enough: it fails 74 % of good trays to catch 90 % of bad ones, falls apart under every perturbation (Section 6.3) and can't localise. Its feature importances were revealing: the top features were low percentiles of CIE b* (roughly, how much bare tray is visible) and the background edge orientations, so the forest is mostly measuring *how much of a tray is in the frame*, not spotting defects. Its one advantage is cost.

**What A still can't do.** On unseen trays, catching about 90 % of defective trays costs about 41 % false rejects; at 80 % recall it drops to about 18 %.

## 5. Validation

### 5.1 What is validated, and how

| Question | Method | Metric |
|---|---|---|
| Is the code right? | Hand-calculated tests; synthetic data with exact labels; cross-check against Ultralytics | Tests pass; mAP agrees within interpolation differences |
| How well are defects localised? | Withheld test split | AP@0.5 per evaluable class, mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95 |
| How good is the tray decision? | Thresholds fixed on validation, applied once to test; bootstrap CIs (1,000 resamples) | FAIL recall, false-reject rate, ROC AUC, escape and review rates |
| How optimistic is the given split? | Same pipeline on the block split | Difference in the above |
| How robust is it? | Perturbed test images, thresholds fixed | Recall and false-reject vs perturbation strength |

mAP is the standard detection measure and includes localisation (IoU ≥ 0.5), but the line acts on trays, so the decision metrics come first: recall on defective trays because escapes are the expensive mistake, and the false-reject rate because that is what running the system costs. Validation picked the best epoch and thresholds, cross-validation on training data picked the baseline's hyper-parameters, and the test split was used once, at the end.

### 5.2 Verification of the implementation

Verification asks whether the code computes what it claims. (i) The metric code passes 21 tests against cases worked out by hand (e.g. predictions TP, FP, TP on 2 ground-truth boxes give AP = 0.5·1 + 0.5·⅔ = 0.833) and against scikit-learn; this caught a real bug, where my first COCO-style AP returned 0.0099 instead of 0 for a detector that never matches. (ii) My mAP@0.5 agrees with the independent Ultralytics validator: 0.547 vs 0.542 (block) and 0.344 vs 0.338 (predefined). (iii) Data loaders are checked by a YOLO↔COCO round trip and a deliberately planted cross-split duplicate. (iv) On the synthetic set the detector reaches mAP@0.5 = 0.978 and a perfect tray ROC, so the lower real-data scores reflect the problem, not the code. (v) Every unsupported input of Section 2.1 is rejected with a reason. All **80 tests** pass on Linux and Windows (`results/test_report.html`), and recomputing the laptop models' mAP on a Linux CPU gives identical numbers.

### 5.3 Results on the real data

**Detection.** On the block split the detector reaches AP@0.5 = 0.871 for `unsealed` and 0.696 for `packaging-error` (at confidence 0.25, precision/recall 0.84/0.75 and 0.69/0.68). Validation mAP (0.765) is close to test (0.783), so choosing the epoch on validation didn't over-fit it. The other three classes have one test box each and aren't reported. Recall at the operating threshold is 0.80–0.92 in every defect-size bin except 0.5–1 % of the image (0.62, n = 16), so small defects aren't systematically missed.

**Tray decision.** With the validation thresholds (*t*<sub>fail</sub> = 0.079, *t*<sub>low</sub> = 0.048) the detector lets 2 of 134 defective trays through (1.5 %), sends 2.9 % to review, and fails 56 % of good trays.

![Error gallery, block split (green = label, red = prediction)](../results/pork-rasher-block/figures/error_gallery.png){width=72%}

**Where it goes wrong.** Missed trays have tiny `packaging-error` boxes at the image edge or on a tray only partly in view. The false rejects are nearly all trays sliding in from the right: the model flags a `packaging-error` on the visible film edge of a tray whose defect, if any, isn't in frame yet, or wasn't labelled in that frame. That is less a detector failure than a modelling one: a *frame* is not a *tray*. Each tray appears in several frames, and the decision should be made once per tray from all of them (Section 7).

### 5.4 How optimistic is the predefined split?

| Pretrained detector, test split | Predefined (leaky) | Block (leakage-aware) |
|---|---|---|
| Tray ROC AUC | 0.924 [0.80, 1.00] | **0.862** [0.78, 0.92] |
| False-reject rate at recall ≈ 0.90 | 0.08 [0.00, 0.29] | **0.41** [0.26, 0.56] |
| mAP@0.5, evaluable classes | 0.589 | 0.783 |
| Good trays in test | 12 | 39 |

At tray level things moved as expected: on unseen trays the decision is clearly worse, and the predefined split's false-reject estimate (1 of 12 good trays) would have badly oversold the system. Detection AP, though, went *up*, which I didn't expect. Two effects are tangled and this data can't separate them: the block test set is made up differently (98 vs 23 `packaging-error` boxes), and the predefined test set is so small that its AP swings on one or two detections. So the conclusion is narrower than "the given split inflates everything": **it can't be used to estimate the false-reject rate**, because its few good trays are near-copies of training frames. The block split is the number an engineer should use.

**What validation cannot establish.** Performance on `wrinkle`, `loose-meat` and `twisted-meat` (0–4 test boxes each); another day, shift, camera, lighting, tray or product (every frame seems to come from one session); whether the labels are right (some `packaging-error` vs `unsealed` boxes look debatable and nobody re-labelled them); and whether a seal actually holds.

## 6. Optimisation and performance

### 6.1 Is it fast enough?

At 60 trays a minute the budget is **1,000 ms per tray**. Timings are single-image and end to end, after warm-up.

| | 256 px | 320 px | **416 px** | 512 px | 640 px |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Laptop CPU, mean / p95 (ms) | 42 / 50 | 48 / 55 | **63 / 80** | 81 / 97 | 103 / 126 |
| Laptop GPU, mean (ms) | 6.3 | 8.2 | **9.2** | 7.3 | 28.9 |
| GFLOPs per image | 1.04 | 1.73 | **2.81** | 4.15 | 6.48 |
| mAP@0.5 evaluable (block test) | 0.728 | 0.749 | **0.783** | 0.741 | 0.691 |

**Yes, on a CPU alone, with about 12× headroom at p95.** I kept 416 px: it is the most accurate, and 640 px is both 1.7× slower and less accurate, most likely because the model was trained at 416 px. GPU timings at batch 1 are mostly fixed per-call overhead and varied between runs on my laptop (9 ms in the final run, 30–40 ms in an earlier one), so the requirement rests on the CPU numbers. Batching lifts GPU throughput from 25 to 94 images/s, useful offline but irrelevant on a line that delivers one tray at a time. Peak memory was 1.8 GB, almost all PyTorch runtime; the weights are 6.5 MB.

### 6.2 FLOPs, arithmetic intensity and the roofline

I counted FLOPs layer by layer with forward hooks: FLOPs = 2·C<sub>out</sub>·H<sub>out</sub>·W<sub>out</sub>·(C<sub>in</sub>/groups)·k<sub>h</sub>·k<sub>w</sub> and bytes = 4·(|input| + |weights| + |output|) per convolution. The counter passes a hand-calculated test and agrees with the independent `thop` counter (2.81 vs 2.85 GFLOPs). Arithmetic intensity ranges from 0.5 to 153 FLOP/byte across the 64 convolutions, 48 for the whole network.

![Roofline on the laptop CPU](../results/pork-rasher-block/figures/roofline.png){width=46%}

My laptop CPU measured 274 GFLOP/s (large matrix multiply) and 19 GB/s (copy bandwidth), a ridge point of about 14 FLOP/byte. The network sits to the right of it, so the roofline says it is **compute-bound** and could run at about 10 ms per image. It manages **47 GFLOP/s (17 % of peak; 59 ms inference)**. The gap is not bandwidth but how inefficiently a CPU runs many small convolutions (short loops, data re-layout, synchronisation per layer); consistent with that, one thread (55 ms) beat fourteen (66 ms) on this hybrid P/E-core chip. Next steps would be a layer-fusing runtime (ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO) or int8 quantisation. The same benchmarks gave 97 GFLOP/s and 4 GB/s in an earlier run, a reminder that laptop power management makes single timings unreliable, which is why I lean on the 12× margin.

**Speeding up the baseline.** `cProfile` showed four functions taking 64 % of the feature-extraction time. Computing each colour conversion once instead of three times, a smaller top-hat footprint and a 32-level GLCM made it **1.9× faster (409 → 214 ms per image)**, on both machines, and a test checks that every feature I didn't mean to change is bit-identical.

### 6.3 Sensitivity and robustness

![Robustness, block split](../results/pork-rasher-block/figures/robustness.png){width=78%}

With thresholds fixed, the detector shrugs off exposure ×0.5–×1.6 (recall 0.97–0.98), synthetic glare and JPEG down to quality 15, which the HSV augmentation covers. **Blur** hurts: at σ = 3 px recall drops from 0.98 to 0.88 and mAP from 0.55 to 0.22. **Losing colour** sends false rejects to 95 %, and heavy noise (σ = 35) suppresses detections (recall 0.75). The scratch model and especially the random forest are far more fragile. So someone has to watch the camera's focus and white balance; a cheap guard is a focus measure (Laplacian variance) and a colour check in the input validation, so such images come back `UNSUPPORTED_INPUT` instead of being scored.

## 7. Limitations and lessons learned

**Main limitations.** Three of five defect classes can't be validated (1–4 test boxes). Everything comes from one recording session. Decisions are made per frame although each tray appears in many frames, and most false rejects are trays half in view. False rejects are too high at high recall (about 41 % at 90 %). Labels weren't independently checked, and a camera can't judge seal strength.

**Lessons learned.**

* **Look at the data before modelling it.** The biggest finding came from reading file names, not from a model. Without it this report would quote an 8 % false-reject rate instead of 41–56 %.
* **Validate what the user acts on.** mAP alone suggests the block-split model is *better*; the tray-level numbers, with their uncertainty, say the opposite, and those are what a plant can use.
* **Verify first, then validate.** Hand-calculated tests caught a real AP bug, and the synthetic set showed the pipeline scores perfect labels perfectly, which is what let me blame the weak real-data numbers on the problem rather than my code.
* **Test on the machine you'll use, early.** Everything ran cleanly on Linux, then broke three times on my Windows laptop. My default Python 3.15 was too new: PyTorch installed, but scikit-image had no ready-made build and wanted a C compiler, so I installed Python 3.12 alongside it. Windows starts worker processes differently, so data loading had to go single-process. A timing step crashed because it used `resource`, which only exists on Linux and macOS. None of this showed up in 80 passing tests, because they hadn't run on Windows yet.
* **A simple baseline earns its place even when it loses**: it showed what a naive model grabs onto and put a number on what the detector adds.

**What I'd improve next.**

1. **Decide per tray, not per frame**: track each tray across frames and fail it only if a defect appears in ≥ *k* of them. This targets the main source of false rejects and can be validated on the existing data.
2. **More, independent data**: other sessions and lighting, the missing defect classes, and a re-labelled sample to measure label noise.
3. **Input guards** for focus and colour (Section 6.3).
4. **Model**: class-balanced sampling for rare classes, and a slightly larger model (YOLOv8s), which the latency margin allows.
5. **Deployment**: ONNX/OpenVINO with int8, and thresholds re-picked on site from the plant's own costs.

## 8. Reflection on the use of AI

*Note to myself before submission: this section has to describe my own use of AI honestly and in my own words. Edit the evaluation so it reflects what I actually checked and understood, then delete this note.*

**How I used it.** Claude (Anthropic), working as an agentic assistant with a cloud workspace and later access to my laptop's project folder, wrote most of the code and tests, proposed the method and validation design, ran the CPU experiments and the synthetic verification, and drafted this report from the generated results. I chose the project, supplied the dataset, ran the GPU pipeline on my laptop, fed errors back and reviewed the outputs. Every commit made by the assistant is marked as co-authored in the history.

**Where it was wrong.** Eight documented cases. A numerical bug: the first AP implementation returned 0.0099 instead of 0, caught by a hand-calculated test. Environment assumptions that only broke on my Windows laptop: a Linux-only module, how Windows starts worker processes, and which Python versions PyTorch and scikit-image support. The Python one cost me most of an evening: install, fail, install 3.12, rebuild, wait for 2.5 GB of PyTorch again. And analysis slips found when reviewing results: a roofline plot mixing GPU timings with a CPU ceiling, a "parallel" timing that was really serial, and run-time estimates that were far too optimistic. Each was fixed and, where possible, turned into a test. The most useful thing it did wasn't code: it noticed from the file names that the images were video frames and measured how badly the given split leaks, which I wouldn't have thought to check.

**Verdict.** With AI I finished a broader and more rigorous project than I could have alone in the time. It was strongest at structure, testing discipline and spotting validation problems, and weakest at assumptions about the environment and at estimates, exactly the things that only fail on a real machine. The risk for me is understanding: code I didn't write is code I still have to explain. Before the presentation I am working through the AP calculation, the YOLO losses and early stopping, the block split and the roofline argument until I can explain them without notes. *[Edit to state what I actually did.]* Next time I'd keep a dated log of prompts and decisions from day one, and run on my own laptop from the start.
